clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive multisystem disorder defined by sulphur-deficient brittle hair, frequently caused by variants in nucleotide excision repair genes such as ERCC2 (XPD), ERCC3 (XPB) or GTF2H5
Hair shows a diagnostic alternating light and dark banding (tiger-tail pattern) under polarised light microscopy
The clinical spectrum is captured by the mnemonic PIBIDS: photosensitivity, ichthyosis, brittle hair, intellectual impairment, decreased fertility and short stature
Photosensitivity occurs in a subset but, unlike xeroderma pigmentosum, is not associated with a raised skin-cancer risk
Neurological features include developmental delay, ataxia and dysmyelination on neuroimaging
Recurrent infections and a tendency to febrile illness are recognised, and some patients have features overlapping immunodeficiency
Analysis of hair amino acid content demonstrates a low cysteine and sulphur level, supporting the diagnosis
Diagnosis integrates the hair microscopy pattern, biochemical hair analysis, DNA-repair testing and molecular confirmation
reference.pathophysiology: Trichothiodystrophy most commonly results from variants affecting components of the transcription factor TFIIH, which functions in both nucleotide excision repair and basal transcription. Impaired TFIIH activity reduces synthesis of cysteine-rich structural proteins of the hair shaft, producing the sulphur deficiency and brittleness, while defective repair and transcription in other tissues account for the neuroectodermal, cutaneous and developmental manifestations. Non-photosensitive forms arise from variants in genes affecting hair-specific structural or regulatory proteins.
additionalDifferentials: Menkes disease and other hair-shaft dysplasias
Other syndromic causes of brittle hair with developmental delay
additionalInvestigations: Polarised light microscopy of the hair shaft for the tiger-tail banding pattern
Biochemical analysis of hair cysteine and sulphur content
Molecular genetic testing including ERCC2, ERCC3 and GTF2H5
Functional DNA-repair assay in photosensitive forms
redFlags: Recurrent or severe infections suggesting associated immune compromise
Failure to thrive or feeding difficulty in infancy
Severe ichthyosis with skin barrier failure in the neonate
reference.prognosis: Outcome varies widely with severity, from early death in severe neonatal ichthyosiform presentations to survival into adulthood with milder disease. Recurrent infection contributes significantly to morbidity and mortality, and care is supportive.
pitfalls: Overlooking the diagnosis without polarised light hair microscopy
Assuming photosensitivity implies xeroderma pigmentosum and a high cancer risk
Missing associated immune deficiency and infection risk
Attributing the brittle hair to an acquired or nutritional cause
management: Recognise there is no curative or disease-specific therapy, so provide coordinated supportive multisystem care tailored to each patient's manifestations
Institute strict photoprotection with broad-spectrum sunscreen, protective clothing and ultraviolet avoidance in the photosensitive subgroup
Manage the ichthyosis with emollients and keratolytics and provide gentle skin and hair care
Treat infections promptly and aggressively, ensure immunisations are up to date and monitor for features of immunodeficiency, given recurrent infection is a major cause of morbidity

Support neurodevelopment with physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech therapy and special educational input for intellectual impairment, ataxia and dysmyelination, alongside nutritional and growth monitoring
Coordinate care through clinical genetics, dermatology, neurology, immunology and paediatrics
Offer genetic counselling and family and prenatal testing, reflecting autosomal recessive inheritance and the nucleotide-excision-repair genes ERCC2, ERCC3 and GTF2H5
